Question:
How many non-empty subsets \(S\) of \(\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 15\}\) have the following two properties?

\((1)\) No two consecutive integers belong to \(S.\)

\((2)\) If \(S\) contains \(k\) elements, then \(S\) contains no number less than \(k.\)
Solution:
Method 1: Remove the required gaps

The lower bound on the selected numbers depends on the subset's size, so first fix that size. Write a valid subset with \(k\) elements as
\[
S=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_k\}.
\]
The conditions become \(a_1\ge k\) and \(a_{i+1}\ge a_i+2\). Therefore
\[
a_k\ge k+2(k-1)=3k-2.
\]
Since \(a_k\le15\), only \(k=1,2,3,4,5\) are possible.

Ordinary combinations count distinct choices without a spacing restriction. To obtain such choices, subtract one extra unit at each successive position:
\[
b_i=a_i-(i-1),\qquad 1\le i\le k.
\]
Because consecutive \(a_i\)'s differ by at least \(2\), consecutive \(b_i\)'s differ by at least \(1\). The endpoint bounds give
\[
k\le b_1<b_2<\cdots<b_k\le16-k.
\]
Thus the \(b_i\)'s form a \(k\)-element subset of the \(17-2k\) integers from \(k\) through \(16-k\).

Conversely, choose any \(k\) distinct integers in this interval, put them in increasing order, and define \(a_i=b_i+(i-1)\). The resulting numbers are at least \(k\), consecutive numbers differ by at least \(2\), and \(a_k\le15\). These constructions undo one another, so every valid subset is counted exactly once. The number of size-\(k\) subsets is therefore
\[
\binom{17-2k}{k}.
\]
The five sizes are disjoint and exhaust all nonempty possibilities. Their total is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\binom{15}{1}+\binom{13}{2}+\binom{11}{3}
+\binom94+\binom75\\
&\qquad=15+78+165+126+21\\
&\qquad=\boxed{405}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The empty subset is excluded because the count starts at \(k=1\). The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).

Method 2: Count by reducing to smaller sets

Removing the largest selected number lowers the subset's size by one. Subtracting one from the remaining numbers then lowers their required minimum by the same amount. This suggests relating the answer to counts for smaller ground sets.

For each integer \(n\ge0\), let \(F(n)\) count the subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfying the two conditions, including the empty subset. For \(n=0\), the ground set is empty. The initial values are
\[
F(0)=1,\qquad F(1)=2,\qquad F(2)=3,
\]
because for \(n=1,2\), only the empty subset and singletons are allowed.

For \(n\ge3\), split the valid subsets according to whether they contain \(n\). Those omitting \(n\) are counted by \(F(n-1)\).

Now take a valid subset containing \(n\), with \(k\) elements. Remove \(n\), then subtract \(1\) from every remaining element. The resulting subset \(T\) has \(k-1\) elements, each at least \(k-1\), and its gaps remain at least \(2\). The original subset could not contain \(n-1\), so the elements of \(T\) are at most \(n-3\). Thus \(T\) is counted by \(F(n-3)\). When the original subset is \(\{n\}\), this gives the empty \(T\).

Conversely, take any subset \(T\) counted by \(F(n-3)\), and let its size be \(j\). Add \(1\) to each element, then adjoin \(n\). The shifted elements are at least \(j+1\), their gaps remain at least \(2\), and they are at most \(n-2\), so none is consecutive to \(n\). Also \(j\le n-3\), which ensures that the adjoined \(n\) is at least the new size \(j+1\). This construction also works for empty \(T\), producing \(\{n\}\).

The two constructions are inverses. Hence the subsets containing \(n\) are counted exactly once by \(F(n-3)\), and the exhaustive, disjoint split gives
\[
F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-3),\qquad n\ge3.
\]
Successive applications yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(3)&=4,\quad F(4)=6,\quad F(5)=9,\\
F(6)&=13,\quad F(7)=19,\quad F(8)=28,\\
F(9)&=41,\quad F(10)=60,\quad F(11)=88,\\
F(12)&=129,\quad F(13)=189,\quad F(14)=277.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(F(15)=277+129=406\). Removing the one empty subset leaves
\[
406-1=\boxed{405},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
